newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Clarke paints picture of stable, successful UK.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Clarke paints picture of stable, successful UK.

text.p: Finance minister Kenneth Clarke on Wednesday painted himself as a level-headed manager of Britain's economy after delivering a budget which ignored calls by right-wingers in his Conservative Party for large tax cuts.

He said a budget that delivered modest fiscal tightening meant policy was not too loose for an economy that is recovering steadily. But if inflationary pressures emerge, he said he would not hesitate to raise interest rates.
"I will do whatever is necessary but at the moment there are a lack of inflation pressures," Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke told a post-budget press briefing.
"As soon as they show signs of rising I will act."

Earlier, Clarke said his budget would deliver continued economic growth, just what the electorate wanted. With elections less than six months away, many Conservatives had clamoured for deeper tax cuts than the one penny Clarke sliced off income tax.
"We are now a stable, successful economy, and this is a sensible, virtuous budget," he declared.
The budget, announced on Tuesday, contained a voter-pleasing cut in the basic rate of income tax to 23 percent and modest spending increases in the popular key areas of health and education.
But the cuts were almost balanced by higher taxes on petrol and tobacco products and plans to close tax loopholes and end certain allowances.
"Never forget, good economics is good politics," Clarke said in his budget speech, an apparent reproof to those who said only huge tax cuts would rescue their party from deep unpopularity.

Opinion polls put the Conservatives some 20 points behind the opposition Labour Party, with an election due by May 22. No party in British polling history has climbed such a huge electoral mountain in so short a time.

A post-budget poll published on Wednesday showed that Britons were apparently unimpressed by Clarke's budget. The NOP poll, published in the Evening Standard newspaper, said eight out of 10 Britons thought the budget would leave them worse off or make no difference.

But Clarke, in a BBC radio interview, said once electors contemplated the transformation in the British economy since the Conservatives came to power in 1979 they would see powerful reasons for voting again for the ruling party.
Bookmakers Ladbrokes cut their odds on the Conservatives retaining power to 6-4 from 7-4 after the budget.
The Chancellor also rejected suggestions that his budget was too cautious because he was keeping one eye on the criteria laid down for government debt in the European Union's Maastricht Treaty.
The treaty makes various demands on countries wishing to join a single European currency -- including a budget deficit of no more than three percent of national income.
"I have not drawn up the budget to aim at the Maastricht criteria," Clarke said, adding that it was a coincidence that his budget had forecast that Britain would meet the targets.

He said his budget contained "some good news...some bad news" for ordinary people, but on balance cut the tax burden on the average family. "Last year, the same mixture produced one of the best economic years we have ever had, and so this budget is going to as well," he said.
He forecast economic growth of 3.5 percent next year.

Labour leader Tony Blair, speaking on the same programme, said his party would not vote against the income tax cut, since voters needed some relief from the higher taxes which the Conservatives have introduced since the last election in 1992.
Blair said the cumulative effect of tax rises since 1992 were equivalent to seven percentage points on income tax.

Labour have avoided pledges which may give the Conservatives an opportunity to portray it as the party of higher taxation, a ploy used by the Conservatives with devastating effect at the 1992 election.
